newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-EASY PICKINGS FOR HINGIS AND COMPANY.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-EASY PICKINGS FOR HINGIS AND COMPANY.

text.p: The French Open, traditionally known for its patient baseline rallies and marathon claycourt battles, was transformed into fast-forward mode at Roland Garros on Saturday.

A series of mis-matches and two unfortunate injuries combined to produce one of the briefest day's entertainment in recent Grand Slam memory but there were no complaints from either Martina Hingis, Monica Seles, Mary Pierce or Michael Chang.

On a sunny afternoon when it sometimes appeared only players with a first name beginning with M stood a chance of victory, all four progressed to the last 16 without dropping a set or, in some cases, breaking into a sweat.
Hingis, the women's world number one, was arguably the most impressive of the quartet, flattening her teenage rival Anna Kournikova 6-1 6-3 to maintain her unbeaten record this year.
The combined age of the two players on centre court was only 31 years and it seemed at one stage as though the match might span a similar number of minutes.

Kournikova was powerless against the variety of Hingis's strokes and eventually held out for only 42 minutes in what had been billed as a showdown between two potential champions of the next millennium.

"I try to spend as little time on the court as I can, but physically I'm okay," said Hingis, sidelined for six weeks with a knee injury after falling from a horse last month. "I felt pretty strong today."
She now meets 16th seed Barbara Paulus of Austria in the fourth round on Sunday.

Seles, a triple French champion between 1990 and 1992, required 51 minutes to steamroller Nathalie Tauziat 6-0 6-1, being detained only briefly at the end of the first set when the French player saved six set points.

The contest was so one-sided that when Tauziat finally won a game midway through the second set she raised her arms aloft in mock triumph, but Seles was already looking ahead to a last 16 match against Pierce.
The French 10th seed dropped only four games against compatriot Sandrine Testud and Seles, once renowned as the hardest hitter in the women's game, is wary of her rival's power.
"I can't play defensively against Mary because she hits the ball really hard," said Seles. "She'll just blow me off the court."
Sixth seed Arantxa Sanchez Vicario was another rapid winner, 6-0 6-3 over Dominique Van Roost of Belgium, and now meets Natasha Zvereva who downed 14th seed Brenda Schultz-McCarthy 7-6 6-4.
The Spaniard's performance certainly encouraged those tempted to put money on a repeat of the 1989 French Open where Sanchez Vicario and Chang secured their first Grand Slam triumphs.

Chang, the only American left in the men's draw, disposed of his third successive French opponent when Stephane Simian retired with a groin strain at 5-2 in the second set and looks in an increasingly determined mood.
"It's been a very French French Open so far, but I don't have any complaints," smiled Chang.
"After only a few games I could see he was hurt. You've got to give him credit for going out there and trying even though he couldn't move very well."

Chang's last 16 opponent, however, is another former champion, Sergi Bruguera of Spain, who breezed past Belgian Dick Norman 6-3 6-1 6-3 in just 87 minutes in what most people saw as a light aperitif to the potential marathon sitting involving Chang.
"There are definitely going to be a lot of long points," said Chang. "Whenever you play Sergi on clay you know it's going to be tough. He's had a lot of success here but I'm looking forward to it."
South African 13th seed Wayne Ferreira did not even make it on court for his third round match against Petr Korda of the Czech Republic.
Ferreira twisted an ankle in practice on Friday, allowing Korda to book his first French Open fourth round berth since reaching the final in 1992.
